at dividere.explanation: "At dividere" means "to divide". To say what you divide by, use "med" (by): "Vi dividerer tallet med to" (We divide the number by two).

at dokumentere.explanation: "At dokumentere" means "to document". It comes from the noun "et dokument" (a document). To say what you prove something with, use "med" (with): "Vi dokumenterer resultaterne med billeder" (We document the results with photos).

at dominere.explanation: "At dominere" means "to dominate". To say a person talks the most in a conversation: "Han dominerer samtalen" (He dominates the conversation). To say a color stands out most in a picture: "Blå dominerer billedet" (Blue dominates the picture).

at donere.explanation: "At donere" means "to donate". To name who receives the gift, add "til" (to): "Jeg donerer penge til Røde Kors" (I donate money to the Red Cross).

at downloade.explanation: "At downloade" means "to download". The Danish verb ends in "e", unlike the English "to download". To say you get an app onto your phone: "Jeg downloader en app" (I download an app).

at drage.explanation: "At drage" means "to draw (a conclusion) / go". To say you benefit from something, use "at drage fordel af" (to benefit from): "Vi drager fordel af den nye metro" (We benefit from the new metro). To say people set off for a place, use "at drage til" (to go to): "De drog til Paris" (They went to Paris).

at drikke.explanation: "At drikke" means "to drink". To offer someone a drink, ask: "Vil du have noget at drikke?" (Would you like something to drink?).

at drille.explanation: "At drille" means "to tease". To say someone is teased in a playful way: "Han driller sine venner" (He teases his friends). Teasing that hurts is "at mobbe" (to bully): "Hun bliver mobbet i skolen" (She is bullied at school).

at drive.explanation: "At drive" means "to run (a business) / drift". To say you run a shop: "Hun driver en butik" (She runs a shop). To say something is carried along by wind or water: "Skyerne driver hen over himlen" (The clouds drift across the sky).

at droppe.explanation: "At droppe" means "to drop / skip". It comes from the English verb "to drop". To say you give up a plan: "Vi dropper planen" (We are dropping the plan).

at drukne.explanation: "At drukne" means "to drown". In the past, use "er" (am/is), not "har" (have): "Manden er druknet" (The man has drowned).

at dryppe.explanation: "At dryppe" means "to drip". To say water falls from something in drops: "Det drypper fra taget" (It drips from the roof). To say you put drops of something on food: "at dryppe citronsaft på fisken" (to drip lemon juice on the fish).

at drysse.explanation: "At drysse" means "to sprinkle". To say what you sprinkle something on, use "på" (on): "Jeg drysser sukker på kagen" (I sprinkle sugar on the cake).

at drøfte.explanation: "At drøfte" means "to discuss". To say you discuss a topic, put the topic straight after it: "Vi drøfter budgettet" (We are discussing the budget). The verb "at tale om" (to talk about) needs "om" (about): "Vi taler om budgettet" (We are talking about the budget).

at drømme.explanation: "At drømme" means "to dream". To say what you dream while asleep, use "om" (about): "Jeg drømte om dig" (I dreamed about you). To say what you wish for in life: "Hun drømmer om at rejse" (She dreams of traveling).

at dufte.explanation: "At dufte" means "to smell (nice)". To say what a smell is like, use "af" (of): "Det dufter af kaffe" (It smells of coffee). For a bad smell, use "at lugte" (to smell): "Det lugter af fisk" (It smells of fish).

at duge.explanation: "At duge" means "to be any good / work". To say something will not do: "Det duer ikke" (That will not do). To say a tool is no good for a job, use "til" (for): "Den kniv duer ikke til brød" (That knife is no good for bread). A mix-up: "duer" is also the plural of "en due" (a dove): "Duerne sidder på taget" (The doves sit on the roof).

at dukke op.explanation: "At dukke op" means "to show up". To say someone did not come to an event: "Han dukkede ikke op til mødet" (He did not show up for the meeting). To say something appears on a screen, it means "to pop up": "En besked dukker op" (A message pops up).

at dumpe.explanation: "At dumpe" means "to fail (an exam)". To say which exam, use "til" (at): "Han dumpede til eksamen" (He failed the exam). The opposite is "at bestå" (to pass): "Hun bestod eksamen" (She passed the exam).

at dykke.explanation: "At dykke" means "to dive", as in going under water: "Vi dykker ved koralrevet" (We dive at the coral reef). To dive in headfirst from a board, say "at stupe" (to dive in): "Han stuper fra vippen" (He dives from the board).

at dyppe.explanation: "At dyppe" means "to dip". To leave something in water for a long time, use "at lægge i blød" (to soak): "Jeg lægger bønnerne i blød" (I soak the beans).

at dyrke.explanation: "At dyrke" means "to grow / practice (a sport)". To say you grow plants on purpose: "Vi dyrker tomater" (We grow tomatoes). To say you do a hobby or sport: "Jeg dyrker yoga" (I do yoga).

at dyrke sport.explanation: "At dyrke sport" means "to do sports". It is built from "at dyrke" (to practice) and "sport" (sports). To say you play one named ball sport, use "at spille" (to play): "Jeg spiller tennis" (I play tennis).

at dække.explanation: "At dække" means "to cover". To say an insurance company pays for a loss: "Forsikringen dækker skaden" (The insurance covers the damage).

at dække bord.explanation: "At dække bord" means "to set the table". It is built from "at dække" (to cover) and "bord" (table). To ask someone to help before dinner: "Kan du dække bord til aftensmad?" (Can you set the table for dinner?)

at dække over.explanation: "At dække over" means "to cover up", as in keeping a mistake hidden. To say you protect someone by staying quiet about what they did: "Hun dækkede over sin bror" (She covered for her brother).

at dæmpe.explanation: "At dæmpe" means "to dampen / turn down". To say you make a light softer: "Vi dæmper lyset" (We dim the lights). To tell a person to tone it down: "Dæmp dig!" (Tone it down!)

at døbe.explanation: "At døbe" means "to baptize". To say someone was baptized with a name: "Hun blev døbt Maria" (She was baptized Maria). To say you gave a name to an animal: "Vi døbte hunden Bølle" (We named the dog Bølle).

at dømme.explanation: "At dømme" means "to judge / sentence". To say a court found someone guilty, use "for" (for) with the crime: "Han blev dømt for tyveri" (He was convicted of theft). To say you form an opinion of people: "Man skal ikke dømme folk på udseendet" (You should not judge people by their looks).

dagen efter.explanation: "Dagen efter" means "the day after". To say which day it was, name the earlier event after it: "dagen efter eksamen" (the day after the exam). To say the next day without naming an event, use "næste dag" (next day): "Næste dag tog vi hjem" (The next day we went home).

dagens ret.explanation: "Dagens ret" means "dish of the day". It is built from "dagens" (the day's) and "ret" (dish). To ask a waiter about it: "Hvad er dagens ret?" (What is the dish of the day?)

dagevis.explanation: "Dagevis" means "for days". The ending "-vis" works the same in other words, such as "timevis" (for hours) and "ugevis" (for weeks).

dagligdags.explanation: "Dagligdags" means "everyday". To talk about the language people use in normal conversation, use it with "sprog" (language): "dagligdags sprog" (everyday language). A mix-up: "daglig" (daily) says something happens each day, as in "en daglig tur" (a daily walk). "Dagligdags" says something is ordinary, as in "en dagligdags hændelse" (an everyday event).

dagligt.explanation: "Dagligt" means "daily". To say how often someone does something, put it after the verb: "Jeg læser dagligt" (I read every day). In front of a thing, use "daglig" with an en-word and "dagligt" with an et-word: "en daglig tur" (a daily walk), "et dagligt møde" (a daily meeting).

dagligvarer.explanation: "Dagligvarer" means "the groceries". It is built from "daglig" (daily) and "varer" (goods). In Denmark, two supermarket chains where people buy them are "Netto" and "Føtex".

dagpenge.explanation: "Dagpenge" means "unemployment benefits". Literally, the word means "day money". In Denmark, you only get them if you are a member of an "a-kasse" (an unemployment insurance fund).

dagslys.explanation: "Dagslys" means "daylight". It is built from "dag" (day) and "lys" (light). To say a room is bright enough without lamps: "Der er rigeligt dagslys i stuen" (There is plenty of daylight in the living room).

damp.explanation: "Damp" means "steam". The part "damp" also appears in other words, such as "en dampbåd" (a steamboat) and "en dampmaskine" (a steam engine).

data.explanation: "Data" means "data". To say you collect data, use "at indsamle" (to collect): "Vi indsamler data" (We collect data).

datalogi.explanation: "Datalogi" means "computer science". It is built from "data" (data) and the ending "-logi" (study of). The same ending is in "biologi" (biology) and "psykologi" (psychology).

datid.explanation: "Datid" means "a past tense". To tell someone to use it, say "i datid" (in the past tense): "Skriv sætningen i datid" (Write the sentence in the past tense). For the past as a period of history, use "fortid" (the past): "Vikingerne boede her i fortiden" (The Vikings lived here in the past).

december.explanation: "December" means "December". Danish writes month names with a lowercase letter, so you write "i december" (in December), not "i December". In Denmark, people celebrate Christmas on the evening of 24 December, called "juleaften" (Christmas Eve).

dedikeret.explanation: "Dedikeret" means "dedicated". It comes from the verb "at dedikere" (to dedicate). To say a thing is made for one task only: "en dedikeret server" (a dedicated server).

defekt.explanation: "Defekt" means "defective". To say you can swap a faulty item in a shop: "Du kan bytte en defekt vare" (You can exchange a defective item). A mix-up: "ødelagt" (broken) says something was damaged: "Min telefon er ødelagt" (My phone is broken).

dejlig.explanation: "Dejlig" means "lovely". To say you are glad to meet someone: "Dejligt at møde dig" (Nice to meet you). To say the weather is lovely: "Det er dejligt vejr" (It is lovely weather).

deltagelse.explanation: "Deltagelse" means "participation". It is the noun for the verb "at deltage" (to take part). To thank someone for coming, use "i" (in) before the event: "Tak for din deltagelse i kurset" (Thank you for your participation in the course).

dem.explanation: "Dem" means "them". To say something is done to them: "Jeg hjælper dem" (I help them). To say they do something, use "de" (they): "De ser mig" (They see me).

demokratisk.explanation: "Demokratisk" means "democratic". It comes from the noun "et demokrati" (a democracy). To say people decide something together: "en demokratisk proces" (a democratic process).

den offentlige sektor.explanation: "Den offentlige sektor" means "the public sector". To say someone works somewhere else, use the opposite, "den private sektor" (the private sector): "Min søster arbejder i den private sektor" (My sister works in the private sector).

den tid, den sorg.explanation: "Den tid, den sorg" means "We'll cross that bridge when we come to it". Word for word, it means "that time, that sorrow". To brush off a worry about the future: "Hvad hvis det regner?" "Den tid, den sorg." (What if it rains? We will deal with that if it happens.)

dengang.explanation: "Dengang" means "back then". It is built from "den" (that) and "gang" (time), so it literally means "that time". To say back when something was true, start a clause with it: "dengang jeg var barn" (back when I was a child).

denim.explanation: "Denim" means "denim". Another Danish word for jeans is "cowboybukser" (literally, cowboy trousers). To say what something is made of: "Tasken er lavet af denim" (The bag is made of denim).

denne.explanation: "Denne" means "this" with words that take "en": "denne bil" (this car). For words that take "et", use "dette" (this): "dette hus" (this house). Another way to say the same thing with an en-word is "den her bil" (this car).

deprimerende.explanation: "Deprimerende" means "depressing". To say what causes the feeling: "en deprimerende film" (a depressing movie). To say how a person feels, use "deprimeret" (depressed): "Jeg er deprimeret" (I am depressed).

deprimeret.explanation: "Deprimeret" means "depressed". To say how long a person has felt this way: "Hun har været deprimeret i flere måneder" (She has been depressed for months). To say what causes the feeling, use "deprimerende" (depressing): "en deprimerende film" (a depressing movie).

der.explanation: "Der" means "there". To say where someone is: "Han er der" (He is there). For the place where you are, use "her" (here): "Han er her" (He is here). To say something exists, start the sentence with it: "Der er mange børn" (There are many children). In the middle of a sentence it can also mean "who": "manden, der bor her" (the man who lives here).

der er ingen ko på isen.explanation: "Der er ingen ko på isen" means "There is nothing to worry about". Word for word, it says there is no cow on the ice. To say there is trouble, take away "ingen" (no): "Der er ko på isen" (There is trouble).

derfor.explanation: "Derfor" means "that is why". To give the reason first and the result second: "Jeg er syg, derfor bliver jeg hjemme" (I am sick, that is why I am staying home). To give the result first, use "fordi" (because): "Jeg bliver hjemme, fordi jeg er syg" (I am staying home because I am sick).

derfra.explanation: "Derfra" means "from there". It is built from "der" (there) and "fra" (from). To say you are a stranger to a place, use "herfra" (from here): "Jeg er ikke herfra" (I am not from here). To say where your family comes from: "Min familie kommer derfra" (My family comes from there).

derhen.explanation: "Derhen" means "there". To say you go toward a place, use it after the verb: "Vi cykler derhen" (We cycle there). To name the place where a person stays, use "der" (there): "Han er der" (He is there).

derhjemme.explanation: "Derhjemme" means "at home". To talk about home when you are somewhere else: "Hvad spiser I derhjemme?" (What do you eat at home?). To say you are in your house right now, use "hjemme" (at home): "Jeg er hjemme" (I am at home).

derimod.explanation: "Derimod" means "on the other hand". It shows a contrast with what was just said. To put the contrast after the verb: "Min bror er høj. Jeg er derimod lav." (My brother is tall. I, on the other hand, am short.) To put it right after the person: "Min søster derimod er lav" (My sister, on the other hand, is short).

derinde.explanation: "Derinde" means "in there". It is built from "der" (there) and "inde" (inside). To say where someone is in another room: "Katten er derinde" (The cat is in there). For the room you are in, use "herinde" (in here): "Jeg er herinde" (I am in here).

dermed.explanation: "Dermed" means "with that". It is built from "der" (there) and "med" (with). To say what follows from something you just did: "Han skrev under, og dermed er aftalen indgået" (He signed, and with that the deal is made).

dernede.explanation: "Dernede" means "down there". To say where something is in a lower place: "Katten er dernede" (The cat is down there). For a higher place, use "deroppe" (up there): "Katten er deroppe" (The cat is up there).

dernæst.explanation: "Dernæst" means "next". To list steps in order, say it after "først" (first): "Først kommer maden, dernæst kommer kaffen" (First comes the food, next comes the coffee).

deroppe.explanation: "Deroppe" means "up there". To say where something is in a higher place: "Vores lejlighed ligger deroppe" (Our apartment is up there). For the place where you are, use "heroppe" (up here): "Heroppe er der koldt" (It is cold up here).

derovre.explanation: "Derovre" means "over there". To point to a place at a distance: "Bogen ligger derovre" (The book is over there). To say you go there, use "derover" (over there, with movement): "Jeg går derover" (I am going over there).

derude.explanation: "Derude" means "out there". To say where children are outside: "Børnene er derude" (The children are out there). For inside something, use "derinde" (in there): "Børnene er derinde" (The children are in there).

derudover.explanation: "Derudover" means "in addition". At the start of a sentence, the verb follows right after it: "Derudover er prisen lav" (In addition, the price is low).

design.explanation: "Design" means "design". It is an et-word, as "designet" (the design) shows. To say what field someone works in: "Hun arbejder med design" (She works in design). Danish furniture and lamps are known abroad as "dansk design" (Danish design).

desperat.explanation: "Desperat" means "desperate". To say what a person is desperate to get, use "efter" (for): "Hun er desperat efter et job" (She is desperate for a job).

desuden.explanation: "Desuden" means "besides". To add one more point after a reason: "Huset er for dyrt. Desuden ligger det langt væk." (The house is too expensive. Besides, it is far away.)

desværre.explanation: "Desværre" means "unfortunately". To tell someone bad news: "Desværre er butikken lukket" (Unfortunately the shop is closed).

det.explanation: "Det" means "it". It stands for a thing that takes "et": "Jeg har et hus, og det er stort" (I have a house, and it is big). Things that take "en" use "den": "Jeg har en bil, og den er stor" (I have a car, and it is big). When you point to something just said or done, it means "that": "Det er sjovt" (That is fun). When there is no particular thing, such as weather: "Det regner" (It is raining).

det er.explanation: "Det er" means "it is". To name or describe a thing: "Det er en bog" (It is a book). To point at someone and say who they are, it means "that is": "Det er min bror" (That is my brother).

det er en god idé.explanation: "Det er en god idé" means "That's a good idea". To agree with a suggestion: "Skal vi gå en tur?" "Det er en god idé." (Shall we go for a walk? That's a good idea.) The short form is "God idé!" (Good idea!).

det er hip som hap.explanation: "Det er hip som hap" means "It's all the same". To say you do not mind which option is chosen: "Kaffe eller te?" "Det er hip som hap." (Coffee or tea? Either is fine.)

det er i orden.explanation: "Det er i orden" means "It's okay". To agree to a plan: "Vi ses klokken otte?" "Det er i orden." (See you at eight? That's fine.) Literally, "i orden" means "in order".

det er ikke så svært.explanation: "Det er ikke så svært" means "It's not that hard". It is built from "svært" (difficult) and "ikke så" (not so). To reassure someone who is stuck: "Jeg kan ikke finde ud af det." "Det er ikke så svært." (I cannot figure it out. It's not that hard.)

det er lige det.explanation: "Det er lige det" means "Yes, that's exactly it". To confirm that someone has understood you: "Du mener, at vi skal vente?" "Det er lige det." (You mean we should wait? That's exactly it.) Said short, "lige det" means "exactly that": "Jeg ville have lige det" (I wanted exactly that).

det er lige meget.explanation: "Det er lige meget" means "It doesn't matter". To say you do not mind which option is chosen: "Pizza eller pasta?" "Det er lige meget." (Pizza or pasta? It doesn't matter.) To say "I don't care", add "mig" (me): "Det er mig lige meget". This can sound rude.

det er min skyld.explanation: "Det er min skyld" means "It's my fault". To blame someone else, change "min" (my) to "hans" (his): "Det er hans skyld" (It's his fault).

det er rigtigt.explanation: "Det er rigtigt" means "That's right". To agree that something is correct: "Er mødet klokken ti?" "Ja, det er rigtigt." (Is the meeting at ten? Yes, that's right.) A mix-up: "rigtig" before another word means "really", as in "rigtig godt" (really good).

det er synd.explanation: "Det er synd" means "That's a shame". To answer bad news: "Hun er syg i dag." "Åh, det er synd." (She is sick today. Oh, that's a shame.) To name the person you feel sorry for, add "for" (for): "Det er synd for dig" (That's too bad for you).
